The participants in the study are already flagged on the NHS Digital system, therefore the customer does not need to send in the cohort again.  No new data is required under this Agreement.

Under previous iterations of this Agreement, NHS Digital provided regular updates on participant events including removals and re-entries to NHS registration, cancer registrations and deaths, including cause of death details. The data supplied initially included directly identifying data items (e.g. names, NHS numbers, dates of birth, etc.) but from 2017 onwards, the data released by NHS Digital was pseudonymised and this will not be linked to the identifying data held in any way.

NHS Digital provided the University of Oxford with month and year and causes of deaths and month and year and diagnosis of cancer and a unique study ID. 

The Senior Statistician within the Cancer Epidemiology Unit (CEU) at the University of Oxford linked the data, using Study ID, with study participants’ pseudonymised questionnaire records. All subsequent analyses use only subsets of the pseudonymised data.  All such subsets are customised according to the characteristics relevant to the specific analysis containing only the minimum data required for the specific purpose.

Various types of analyses are undertaken on an on-going basis for the overarching purpose of assessing cancer incidence and overall mortality. The data will be held only at the Cancer Epidemiology Unit at the University of Oxford. The datasets will be pseudonymised as described above before statistical analyses are undertaken.

The study will not share any data supplied by NHS Digital with any other institution or individual outside of the study team at Oxford University.

All users of the data are substantive employees of the University of Oxford.

Data supplied by NHS Digital and existing data will be kept in separate electronic files linked by a numerical, anonymous subject identifier. Lifestyle/dietary data required for analysis will be extracted from the relevant data files (which do not contain subject names, NHS numbers or full dates of birth) and merged with the data supplied by NHS Digital using the subject identifier, without having recourse to any identifiable data.

The aim of the study is to improve information on diet in relation to the risk of cancer and cardiovascular disease and offers potential for improvements in public health in the UK. The results are published in peer-reviewed publications and presented at conferences, and are also reported through national media.

University of Oxford research relates directly to the health of 1.2 million people in the UK who follow vegetarian diets (NHS 2014). The long-term effects on cancer of a vegetarian diet are not well understood, and little is known about the health effects of a vegan diet. Our previous research has demonstrated lower risks of obesity (50%), heart disease (30%), stomach cancer (60%) and haematological cancers (36%) in vegetarians compared with non-vegetarians (Key and Davey 1996, Crowe et al 2013, Key et al 2009, 2014), and further study is likely to reveal other associations between diet and cancer risk. As well as peer-reviewed scientific publications, where appropriate, University of Oxford will also communicate with the NHS and other organisations such as the National Cancer Intelligence Network within Public Health England and other health providers in the UK, where the outputs from the study will provide information to underpin their health advice to the public. 

For example:  The PI of this study sits on the Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition (SACN) which reports to Public Health England and other UK government organisations. Conclusions from this committee are used to formulate government and NHS policy on diet and thus reduce the risk of disease and the burden on the NHS. In a current SACN update, the fortification of the UK food supply for folic acid to prevent neural tube defects included a key piece of evidence including data from the Oxford Vegetarian Study, related to the safety of folic acid with respect to cancer risk. (https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/consultation-on-draft-sacn-update-on-folic-acid). 

Future work will look at  heart disease (further analyses with more data), death from stroke and risk of prostate cancer, as well as the protective impact of vegetarian diets in preventing the development of obesity. 

In the planned new analyses of ischaemic heart disease and stroke, the study will use their data on diet to estimate the impacts on health of replacing energy (calories) from red and processed meat with energy from plant foods which can be used to replace these foods, such as legumes (beans, peas and lentils) and nuts. 

The NHS Choices website (http://www.nhs.uk/Livewell/Vegetarianhealth/Pages/Vegetarianhealthqanda.aspx#what) states that “a vegetarian diet can be very healthy” and reports on an NHS patient who comments “I feel much healthier on a vegan diet”, but includes few specific statements about the benefits. The research will provide the robust information needed to include more specific facts and advice on the NHS website and thus enable the public to improve their health and reduce the burden on the NHS.

As well as peer-reviewed scientific publications, where appropriate, University of Oxford will also communicate with the NHS and other organisations such as the National Cancer Intelligence Network within Public Health England where the outputs from the study will provide information to underpin their health advice to the public.

This study will directly benefit health care through the NHS by providing clinicians and other NHS health care professionals with up-to-date evidence-based guidance on the effects of diet on cancer and the risk of death. This will improve clinical health care and inform planners and policy makers to address demands on health and social care in the present and future.

The robust, reliable knowledge on vegetarian diets and risk of chronic disease will provide the evidence to underpin the judgements made by decision-makers on the future direction of NHS policy in relation to dietary advice, thus acting as an enabler.  For example, the NHS reported in 2013 that a vegetarian diet brings a range of health benefits and is linked to longer lifespan (12% in risk of death from any cause, see http://www.nhs.uk/news/2013/06June/Pages/Vegetarian-diet-linked-to-longer-lifespan.aspx).  This NHS assessment noted that the study concerned had a relatively short follow-up of six years, this is quite short to address how dietary patterns might affect the risk of death. 

In University of Oxford analyses, there is a follow-up of over thirty years which will provide the NHS with much more reliable information on the long-term health of people following a vegetarian diet. This reliable evidence will be available in publications in late 2017 and 2018, enabling updating of NHS sources during 2018. 

In the link http://www.nhs.uk/news/2013/01january/pages/does-a-veggie-diet-lead-to-a-healthier-heart.aspx
The  researchers concluded that vegetarians had a 32% lower risk of IHD than non-vegetarians, and that this is likely due to “reduced levels of well-established risk factors for IHD, such as non-HDL cholesterol concentrations and systolic blood pressure”. This large and impressive prospective cohort study suggests that a vegetarian diet may benefit your heart; reducing the risk of IHD. This was a well-conducted, large long-term study that suggests there are heart healthy benefits to a vegetarian diet. The NHS will be able to continue to use University of Oxford data to update their websites accessible to the general public.

This NHS provided advice, based on OVS data, to their stakeholders. This will enable commissioners to implement appropriate policies in relation to diet, thus reducing the financial burden of dietary related diseases. 

More recently one of the named researchers attended the inaugural workshop of the Cancer and Nutrition NIHR infrastructure collaboration http://cancerandnutrition.nihr.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Cancer-Nutrition-Full-Report-FINAL_03-06-16.pdf . OVS and EPIC will be part of this initiative. The Cancer and Nutrition NIHR infrastructure collaboration will improve cancer prevention and care for clinicians and patients.

Key TJ, Appleby PN, Crowe FL, Bradbury KE, Schmidt JA, Travis RC. Cancer in British vegetarians: updated analyses of 4998 incident cancers in a cohort of 32,491 meat eaters, 8612 fish eaters, 18,298 vegetarians, and 2246 vegans. Am J Clin Nutr 2014;100 Suppl 1:378S-85S.

states.objective:
The University of Oxford requires ongoing access to data supplied by NHS Digital (and predecessor organisations) for the purpose of a research study known as The Oxford Vegetarian Study (OVS).  OVS, also known as the Study of Cancer in Vegetarians, was designed in 1980, and the 11,040 participants were recruited through the Vegetarian Society, media and by word of mouth between 1980 and 1984. Participants implicitly consented to the study by voluntarily completing and returning the questionnaire. 

The aim of the study is to investigate the long-term health of vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians, examining cancer risk and mortality. The design is an observational cohort, based on recruiting healthy volunteer participants and following their long-term health through linkage to NHS information on incident cancers and causes of death. 

Participants in the study were immediately flagged for cancers and deaths with the Office for National Statistics (ONS)  Record linkage for supplying information for the Study of Cancer in Vegetarians (Ref: MR126). Deaths and cancer information was approved via ONS to supply this information from 1980 to 2013. 
In November/ December 2015 the study received Ethics (NHS REC) and Section 251 (CAG) approval.

There have been 1108 incident cancers (to 31/12/2012) and 1955 deaths (to 31/3/2014) in the cohort. Analysis of the cohort has led to many publications, as recently as 2014, in peer reviewed journals such as the British Medical Journal and British Journal of Cancer.

Data was initially collected by questionnaires on diet and lifestyle, returned by post in 1980-1984. The OVS is supported by a grant from the Medical Research Council (MRC) (“Health of Vegetarians”). 
The study is needed to improve understanding of the effects of diet on health and thus inform advice to governments, health professionals and the public about dietary choices to maximise the potential for long-term good health.

The study is on-going and funding is in place until 2020.  As outlined in the specific outputs analysis of the data will continue into 2018 and the research findings will be presented in 2019.

states.expected_benefits:
The findings of this research study are expected to contribute to evidence-based decision-making for policy-makers, local decision-makers such as doctors, and patients to inform best practice to improve the care, treatment and experience of health care users relevant to the subject matter of the study.

The use of the data could:
- Help the system to better understand the health and care needs of populations by providing robust evidence on the long-term health outcomes of vegetarians and vegans compared to non-vegetarians.

- Advance understanding of the need for, or effectiveness of, preventative health and care measures by assessing how plant-based diets influence cancer and cardiovascular disease risk, supporting strategies to reduce disease burden.

- Inform planning of health services and programmes by enabling policy-makers and commissioners to design dietary guidance and interventions that improve equity of access, experience, and outcomes for diverse populations.

- Lead to the identification or improvement of interventions by clarifying which dietary patterns are associated with reduced risk of chronic conditions, informing NHS dietary advice and public health campaigns.

- Advance understanding of regional and national trends in health and social care needs through analysis of large cohorts and linkage to NHS data, supporting evidence-based decision-making at scale.

- Support knowledge creation and exploratory research that underpins innovations in nutrition science and informs future preventive health strategies.

The findings of this research are expected to deliver direct benefits to patients by providing accurate, evidence-based dietary guidance that supports informed choices about vegetarian and plant-based diets. This will help reduce the risk of cancer and cardiovascular disease through improved prevention strategies and updated NHS dietary advice. Patients will experience better health outcomes and care quality as clinicians use these findings to guide treatment and lifestyle recommendations. Ultimately, the research empowers patients with reliable information for self-care, contributing to healthier lifestyles and a reduction in diet-related conditions.

It is hoped that through publication of findings in peer-reviewed journals and presentations at major conferences, the research will add to the body of evidence considered by policy-making bodies such as the Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition (SACN), the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), and individual clinicians when making treatment decisions. These outputs will inform updates to NHS dietary guidance and public health recommendations, enabling commissioners and practitioners to implement preventive strategies that reduce cancer and cardiovascular risk.
Clients and stakeholders will need to take action based on the evidence provided to realise these benefits. For example, NHS England and SACN may update national dietary guidelines to encourage plant-based eating patterns, which could lead to improved population health outcomes and reduced disease burden on the NHS.

To optimise the potential public benefits, the research team will publish findings in peer-reviewed open-access journals and present them at major national and international conferences to reach academic and clinical audiences. They will engage directly with policy-making bodies such as SACN and OHID to inform updates to NHS dietary guidance and public health recommendations. Where findings warrant wider attention, media engagement and public promotion will be undertaken, including press releases and updates to NHS Choices. Briefing documents will be shared with funders and relevant stakeholders, and collaboration with charities and professional societies in nutrition and cancer research will help ensure the findings are disseminated broadly and applied effectively.

states.objective:
The University of Oxford requires access to NHS England data for the purpose of the following research project: 

Study of Cancer in Vegetarians.

The following is a summary of the aims of the research project provided by University of Oxford:

The Oxford Vegetarian Study (OVS), also known as the Study of Cancer in Vegetarians, is a landmark observational cohort study initiated in 1980 by the University of Oxford. Between 1980 and 1984, the study recruited 11,040 participants through the Vegetarian Society, media campaigns, and word of mouth. Participants implicitly consented by voluntarily completing and returning a detailed dietary questionnaire. The cohort included vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians, enabling long-term comparisons of health outcomes. All recruitment and follow-up data collection have been completed, and the current application seeks permission to retain data until the end of the Data Sharing Agreement for extended analysis.

The project aims to investigate the long-term health effects of vegetarian diets, focusing on cancer risk and mortality. Participants were flagged for cancer and death notifications via Office for National Statistics (ONS) record linkage, and data from ONS MRIS has been received from 1980 through 2017. Initially, data included identifiable items (e.g., names, NHS numbers), but since 2017, NHS England has supplied pseudonymised data, stored separately from the identifiers.

The aim of  the research project is:
- To investigate the long-term health effects of vegetarian and non-vegetarian diets, with a particular focus on cancer incidence and mortality.

The research objectives are:
- Assess cancer risk among vegetarians compared to non-vegetarians using linked cancer registry data.
- Evaluate mortality patterns for major causes of death, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions.
- Analyse dietary factors such as meat, fish, and plant-based food consumption and their association with disease outcomes.

The following NHS England Data will be accessed: 
- MRIS - Cohort Event Notification Report
- MRIS - Cause of Death Report
- MRIS - Members and Postings Report

The MRIS data was requested because it contains official, longitudinal records of cancer incidence and mortality for the Study cohort. This information is essential to achieve the study’s aim of examining the long-term health of vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians. By linking participants’ dietary data to verified NHS and ONS records, researchers can accurately analyse cancer risk and causes of death over several decades. 

The level of the Data will be:

- Identifiable - Necessary because identifiable data is required to accurately link historical study records with NHS cancer and death registrations before pseudonymisation for analysis. Without the identifiers, linkage would be unreliable and compromise research validity. 

The Data will be minimised as follows:
-  Limited to a study cohort of  10,626 participants residing in England and Wales who were originally recruited for the Oxford Vegetarian Study.

University of Oxford is the research sponsor and the controller as the organisation responsible for ensuring that the Data will only be processed for the purpose described above.

The lawful basis for processing personal data under the UK GDPR is:
Article 6(1)(e) - processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller;

The lawful basis for processing special category data under the UK GDPR is:
Article 9(2)(j) - processing is necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes in accordance with Article 89(1) based on Union or Member State law which shall be proportionate to the aim pursued, respect the essence of the right to data protection and provide for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and the interests of the data subject.

This processing is in the public interest because it adheres to the UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research, which protects and promotes the interests of patients, service users and the public, and aims to produce generalisable and publicly available information to inform future decisions over patients’ treatments or care.

The funding comes from multiple sources. Current funders include:

- Medical Research Council
-  World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF) 

The funding is specifically for the research project described.

The funders will have no ability to suppress or otherwise limit the publication of findings.

The study was designed in 1980 as an observational cohort to investigate the long-term health of vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians, focusing on cancer risk and mortality. Recruitment was through the Vegetarian Society of the UK, publicity in local and national media, and word of mouth between 1980 and 1984. Participants joined by voluntarily completing and returning a diet and lifestyle questionnaire. Public benefit was considered in the rationale: the study aimed to provide evidence for health professionals and policymakers on dietary risk factors for chronic diseases. Later engagement occurred when participants were informed of findings and invited to join EPIC-Oxford in 1994.

states.yielded_benefits:
OVS was the first large-scale cohort study in the world with both detailed information and blood samples for a large number of vegetarians and otherwise comparable meat-eaters. Major findings from the study are lower cholesterol and body mass index in vegetarians, and a lower risk of several types of chronic disease including cancers.

OVS has now been running for 40 years. Early results from the study showed robustly for the first time that vegetarians have lower LDL cholesterol than meat-eaters due to a lower intake of saturated fat, underpinning more recent work on diet and risk factors for coronary heart disease, and the UK Government's current recommendations on saturated fat intake
https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/saturated-fats-and-health-sacn-report

OVS was one of only eleven cohort studies worldwide used by the UK Government's Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition to conclude that there is adequate evidence that high intakes of dietary fibre have a beneficial impact on health by reducing the risk of coronary heart disease, and leading to the recent increase in the recommended intake of dietary fibre in the UK from 18 g/d of NSP fibre to 30 g/d of AOAC fibre
https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/445503/SACN_Carbohydrates_and_Health.pdf

The use of evidence from OVS in the reports of the UK Government's Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition has enabled the production of authoritative advice on diet to the NHS and the public, leading to large benefits in the health of the nation and reduction of the burden on the NHS.

Work is ongoing on two manuscripts - one methods paper and one results paper for the WCRF-funded vegetarians and cancer consortium and it is anticipated these will be submitted within the next six months.  The first paper has been circulated to all collaborating authors and first results were presented by Dr Yashvee Dunneram at the 14th European Nutrition Conference FENS2023 in Belgrade, Serbia, 14th-17th November 2023.
